transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-10-23 16:00 UTC | Duration: 74m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jamal Ortiz (Redwood SE), Evelyn Park (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (CTO, Nebula), Liam Chen (SRE), Harper Ross (Data Eng), Owen Diaz (ML Eng)

[00:00] Maya Patel: Okay, welcome everyone. thanks for carving time. quick int for folks on the call?
[00:12] Priya Kapoor: Priya here, CTO. we're looking to tighten p99 on our realtime scoring, currently around 450ms avg but tail blows to 1.2s when load and network hiccups happen.
[00:28] Liam Chen: SRE, we see spikes correlated with cross-region hops to our model VPC in us-west-2. also some hotkey storms for certain user prompts.
[00:42] Jamal Ortiz: Got it. Jamal from Redwood infra team. We'll focus on multi-hop trace analysis, kv cache patterns, and quantization tradeoffs. want to confirm streaming vs non-streaming behaviors are both in scope?
[00:56] Priya Kapoor: yes, both — streaming is used in chat UX, non-streaming for batch scoring.
[01:05] Harper Ross: quick context: model is 70B open checkpoint, currently hosted on dedicated infra, quantized to fp16 for throughput. we saw accuracy dip when we tried aggressive int8 quantization in a POC.
[01:21] Evelyn Park: thanks, good to know. we'll talk about int8 profile strategies and per-head calibration.

[01:35] Topics list recap from Jamal: p95 vs p99 split, streaming pipeline (token-level latency), non-streaming end-to-end, network hop contributions, kv cache hit/miss behavior, batching & autoscale, and on-prem/VPC constraints.

[02:02] Maya Patel: can you walk us through a typical request path? do we have a diagram?
[02:10] Owen Diaz: yes — user -> edge LB in us-east -> API gateway -> internal proxy -> model hop in us-west -> gpu host -> response back. sometimes we also call a reranker service in us-central after generation.
[02:28] Jamal Ortiz: that chain is useful. each hop adds queuing jitter. for streaming, token flushes add more small RPCs which multiply hop-level variance.

[02:50] Liam Chen: our tracing shows for some requests 3x retransmits between proxy and model host — packet loss during peak.
[02:59] Jamal Ortiz: yea that will blow p99. two quick levers: 1) reduce cross-region hops via local routing/caching, 2) increase retry/backoff transparency and idempotent streaming paths.

[03:20] Priya Kapoor: what's Redwood's routing options? we need a pattern that keeps data in-region for compliance too.
[03:29] Evelyn Park: Redwood can pin routing by region and tier — policy-based routing. for Dedicated/Private you can deploy model pools in target regions, and we can configure failover to other pools. also prefix KV caching can be regional to reduce cross-region calls.

[03:50] Harper Ross: say more about prefix KV cache — does that cache live on the same host as the model or is it sharded across nodes?
[03:58] Jamal Ortiz: good question. by default we use a sharded in-memory KV cache colocated with model shards for fastest lookup. hotkeys can concentrate traffic on a subset; we pay attention to shard placement and can enable consistent hashing to spread hotkeys.

[04:18] Harper Ross: last week we saw a 10x increase in requests for a specific prompt — it flattened a shard and p99 spiked. what can we do quickly?
[04:27] Jamal Ortiz: short-term: enable kv-prefetch and soft rate-limit on hotkey patterns; medium-term: increase shard replication for hot prefixes and use request hedging for cold vs hot. Also batching tweaks: smaller batch sizes for latency-sensitive routes.

[04:50] Liam Chen: curious about batching tradeoffs — we need to keep p95 tight but also want cost-efficiency. what's the recommended config?
[04:58] Jamal Ortiz: it's workload dependent. for Nebula we saw from your sample traces that median sequence lengths are 60 tokens. for non-streaming scoring, batch sizes 16-32 with sequence-aware batching usually gives best throughput without inflating tail too much. for streaming low-latency chat, continuous batching with small caps (4-8 tokens per micro-batch) keeps latency bounded.

[05:22] Priya Kapoor: can you explain continuous batching briefly?
[05:26] Jamal Ortiz: sure — the runtime holds a small time window (e.g., 5-10ms) to aggregate tokens across concurrent sessions, then dispatches a micro-batch. that amortizes kernel cost but keeps per-token delay small. it's better than naive big batches which add tens of ms at tail.

[05:48] Owen Diaz: does continuous batching play nicely with streaming token flushes? we saw reordering issues earlier.
[05:55] Evelyn Park: we route tokens through session-affine queues; ordering is preserved, but if you absolutely need strict low jitter we can switch to single-token flushes at cost of throughput.

[06:12] Jamal Ortiz: switching gears — quantization. Harper mentioned int8 caused accuracy regressions. we typically recommend mixed strategy: keep attention/kernel sensitive ops in fp16 and quantize matmul paths to int8 with per-channel calibration. that reduces throughput variability while minimizing quality drop.

[06:36] Harper Ross: can you point to a quick experiment to validate int8 safely?
[06:40] Jamal Ortiz: run a shadow pass: run requests against fp16 and int8 in parallel, collect cosine similarity and task-level metrics. Redwood's eval harness can run this at scale. we can supply the harness and a config for head-by-head comparison.

[06:59] Priya Kapoor: how does quantization affect p99? I thought int8 increased throughput but may introduce variance?
[07:06] Jamal Ortiz: int8 usually lowers tail because it reduces per-token compute time; however, if calibration causes variance across sequence lengths or layers, you can see occasional CPU fallback paths or re-quantize steps which add latency. the runtime tries to avoid fallback by selecting stable kernels.

[07:27] Liam Chen: any gotchas for GPUs vs CPU quantized kernels?
[07:31] Jamal Ortiz: GPU int8 support is maturing. on some older CUDA stacks, int8 kernels may be emulated or have lower throughput; FP16 is safest across hardware. for dedicated infra you can pin to GPU SKUs with validated int8 kernel paths.

[07:50] Maya Patel: let's talk measurement. we need end-to-end traces that attribute where the p99 time goes. what artifacts do you need?
[07:58] Jamal Ortiz: we need full distributed traces with spans for edge LB, API gateway, proxy, model host, and any reranker; sample rate at 100% for a 10-minute window around incidents is ideal. also raw tcp-level counters and dmesg if packet loss suspected.

[08:15] Harper Ross: we can pull 24h trace and a 10m incident window. is there a preferred tracing format?
[08:20] Jamal Ortiz: OpenTelemetry traces are ideal. if you only have jaeger or zipkin exports that's fine, we can ingest.

[08:30] Priya Kapoor: data residency question — for on-prem or VPC, can Redwood keep control plane in redwood-cloud while model runtime sits in Nebula VPC?
[08:39] Evelyn Park: yes, Redwood Private supports a split control plane: control plane endpoints in your VPC or a private link, and model runtime in-prem. KMS integration is supported via customer-managed HSM or cloud KMS. we log audit trails to your S3 bucket or syslog collector.

[08:58] Liam Chen: good — we have strict encryption at rest + customer KMS requirement. any latency impact using remote KMS?
[09:05] Jamal Ortiz: minimal. we fetch keys during startup and cache key material; per-request crypto uses local ephemeral keys. only heavy operations (rotations) hit KMS. we'll share our KMS integration notes.

[09:20] Maya Patel: back to network hops — you mentioned hedging and local caches. can Redwood do last-mile caching for high-frequency prompts?
[09:28] Jamal Ortiz: yes, prefix-level caching and TTL-based caches on gateway edge is available. but for high-similarity prompts, semantic caching is trickier because outputs vary; we prefer prefix/KV caching for stable reranker outputs and repeated instructions.

[09:46] Harper Ross: we saw weird behavior: streaming responses occasionally double-send tokens after a reconnect. is that a runtime bug or network artifact?
[09:55] Evelyn Park: likely reconnect semantics. streaming is idempotent at segment boundaries, but without exact resume tokens, clients might re-request. we can add sequence numbers or resume tokens to the stream to dedupe.

[10:12] Owen Diaz: on the topic of retries, how does Ridgeback (internal name) handle hedged requests? are they cancel-on-response or first-complete wins?
[10:20] Jamal Ortiz: first-complete wins; we cancel outstanding in-flight micro-batches. that reduces queuing but we need to ensure cancellation isn't a source of reordering; we have safe cancellation points.

[10:36] Liam Chen: do you have metrics for how hedging affects p95 vs p99?
[10:40] Jamal Ortiz: in our internal labs hedging reduced p99 by ~30% for cross-region scenarios but increased average compute by ~8%. it's a tradeoff: lower tail at modest cost increase.

[10:55] Priya Kapoor: cost tradeoffs are important. show me a concrete scenario for Nebula's workload.
[11:00] Jamal Ortiz: based on your trace sample, we projected: hosted fp16 no-hedge baseline cost X, with hedging p99 drops 35% but cost up 10%. quantize to mixed int8 and enable region-local model pools cuts cost 22% and p99 down 25% vs baseline. we'll run exact numbers once we have full traces.

[11:22] Harper Ross: that sounds promising. what about autoscaling and warm pools? we see cold-start latency.
[11:29] Evelyn Park: Redwood supports warm pools and instant scale-up with warm containers or pre-warmed GPU instances. for strict SLOs we recommend a small always-on pool sized to baseline QPS and burst capacity for peaks. autoscale policies can be schedule or SLA-triggered.

[11:48] Owen Diaz: any tips on model sharding and kv cache sharding for minimizing cross-host traffic?
[11:53] Jamal Ortiz: co-locate KV shards with model shards and route sessions affinity by shard. also use consistent hashing with virtual nodes to smooth hotkey spikes. replication factor 2 for hot prefixes reduces p99 on single-host failures.

[12:12] Priya Kapoor: good. what observability surfaced in Redwood console will help us triage p99?
[12:18] Evelyn Park: per-token latency histograms, per-route p95/p99, token-level cost breakdown, KV hit/miss heatmaps, and per-shard CPU/GPU utilization. plus trace flamegraphs for end-to-end hop attribution. we can onboard your team to the console and set alerting thresholds.

[12:40] Liam Chen: one more security thing — audit logs retention and SSO integration.
[12:44] Maya Patel: Redwood supports SAML SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and audit log retention up to 7 years as an enterprise addon. we'll include exact SLAs in the security pack.

[12:58] Jamal Ortiz: quick pause — we should capture a concrete experiment plan. propose: 1) supply 24h trace + incident 10m window, 2) Redwood runs two controlled runs: A) streaming path with continuous batching + hedging, B) non-streaming scoring with batch sizes 16/32 and int8 mixed quant. collect p50/p95/p99 and per-hop traces.

[13:25] Priya Kapoor: agreed. timeline?
[13:28] Maya Patel: we'll aim to deliver results in ~7 business days after traces provided.

[13:35] Harper Ross: any risk to our production during these tests?
[13:38] Jamal Ortiz: all Redwood runs can be done against shadow endpoints or in your dedicated sandbox, so no production impact.

[13:48] -- Transcript jump --
[25:12] Jamal Ortiz: (deep dive) kernel selection: for seqlen distributions with heavy short sequences, we pick attention kernels optimized for cached KV reuse, which lowers per-token emissions; avoid dynamic shape penalties by padding to small buckets.
[25:40] Harper Ross: padding is ok but wastes tokens, how to balance?
[25:45] Jamal Ortiz: sequence-aware bucketing: bucket sequences in [1-16], [17-64], [65-256] and run separate queues per bucket. that keeps padding overhead low and kernels stable.

[26:10] Liam Chen: regarding network tuning — any TCP stack recommendations?
[26:15] Jamal Ortiz: enable TCP BBR where available, tune socket buffers for high concurrency, and ensure keepalive and window scaling configured for your LB -> model host path. also ECMP can cause packet reordering; prefer flowstickiness for RPC streams.

[26:35] Priya Kapoor: interesting. we use cloud load balancers that do cross-AZ flows, might be reordering.

[36:02] Evelyn Park: we should also consider retraining the model to better support cached prefixes if semantics allow; that increases cache hit rate and reduces compute.

[36:20] Owen Diaz: ok noted.

[38:44] Jamal Ortiz: small detail on streaming: we support chunked transfer with per-chunk seq numbers. adding that will let your gateway dedupe on reconnects and avoid duplicates.

[41:11] Harper Ross: what about per-customer RBAC and multi-tenant isolation in Dedicated mode? any perf hit?
[41:18] Evelyn Park: there's negligible perf hit for logical isolation; physical multi-tenant isolation is optional. Dedicated physically isolates GPU pools. encryption and RBAC are separate layers.

[45:00] Liam Chen: return to hotkey mitigation: do you have heuristics to detect emerging hotkeys and auto-throttle?
[45:06] Jamal Ortiz: yes — runtime collects prefix frequency histograms and can auto-throttle top-N prefixes or spawn extra replicas dynamically when threshold breached.

[50:35] Priya Kapoor: final recap please?
[50:39] Maya Patel: sure — action items: Redwood runs perf runs A/B for streaming vs non-streaming with your traces; Redwood shares security pack and KMS notes; customer provides traces and prompt sets; schedule pilot scoping call. agreed timeline ~7 business days to initial results.

[51:05] Liam Chen: thanks. two questions: can we get cost delta estimates per 1M requests? and can you show a sample dashboard alert?
[51:14] Maya Patel: yes, we'll include cost delta table and screenshot of alert templates.

[51:25] Priya Kapoor: thanks everyone. that's all from us.
[51:29] Maya Patel: great, I'll follow up with calendar invites and upload links.

[51:35] -- informal close chatter --
[73:55] Recording ends.
